questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Other

questions.question: Please explain: *
questions.answer: There was more than one aspect that motivated me to go. Going to South Korea on exchange offered me a range of opportunities that are important to me as a Korean studies student. Language might be  the most important, but I do also feel that the academic opportunities and the cultural experience were equally important.

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: Like I mentioned I am a Korean studies student so that was crucial to me in choosing South Korea.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: I think it was rather easy. The school offers you to join a buddy program where you can get in contact and get help from a Korean student at the university, and otherwise you can go to the international office and speak with them if you need help.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: I had help both from the buddy program I mentioned, the internation office and because I joined a club I could get help from a student there as well.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing on my own

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: What options were available for on campus housing? *
What options were available for meal plans or cooking facilities? *
What should future exchange students know about on campus housing? *
How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer: I used Airbnb. I think if possible it's a good idea to only choose airbnbs with a lot of reviews and perhaps double-check the address on Naver Maps (Korean version of Google Maps, since Google Maps is not as used). Also I would suggest almost looking for a place as early as possible, half a year before is not too early in my opinion, because all the good and cheaper options disappear quickly.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer: I think there is a lot more freedom in living off campus which I think we are typically quite used to as Danes. The down-side is of course that it can be chaotic if your housing off campus is unsatisfactory and another thing is cost. Living off campus is much more expensive.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I had to answer how satisfied I was with the housing available to students but I have never lived on campus so I just chose 3.

questions.question: How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: How you register I thought was easy to understand because they sent a very thorough guide on how to do it.

questions.question: Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: You start with figuring out which classes you want to take, note down the course number and then on registration day you have to be ready to log into the site. Ewha makes you input your personal info before you are able to register courses, and then you register the classes one class at a time. It is honestly a very stressful process, because registering for classes is like wanting to buy concert tickets and in my case it felt like having to buy 5 concert tickets because I was taking 5 courses.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: Like I mentioned we got a guide that explained the registration process.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: I got up a few hours early in the morning and was actually sitting on the registration site watching the countdown, and I think that might have contributed to me being so lucky that I got everything I wanted. However, at the same time I talked with a few people who weren't as lucky so I think luck also plays a part.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Get up early and prepare a list of the courses you want and in case you might not get them prepare back-up courses as well. I got the courses I wanted but one of them was a back-up course because another was full. I don't think you can see it before on registration day but in some courses there are a limited amount of spots for international students. My friend even went to a PC room to ensure she got the courses she wanted because the internet connection is better there, so it is worth considering.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Did you take BA or MA courses at your host university? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer:
It was quite interesting in comparison to the courses I have taken back at home in Denmark. In Denmark I have had one longer written assignment that determined my grade but in Korea it was determined by multiple tests, multiple written assignments (but they were shorter), attendance, presentations and participation in class. 
With that said I do think the level was similar to Copenhagen University. But I did distinctly feel a difference in workload, in Denmark I think it gets more intense near the end of the semster, while in Korea one thing was constantly replaced by another but it was less intense.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: Because Korean studies has a smaller number of students we have the necessary time to talk and discuss things during class so class participation in not uncommon. However, I have never had so much class participation and groupwork as I feel I did in Korea, but that might also just have had something to do with the courses I chose.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
World Women Through English
K-MOOC: Identity, Agency, Equality, and Security in the Age of AI
Current Issues 
Contemporary Photography
Social Problems in Contemporary Global World

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your second semester. *
What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
K-MOOC is an online course but you learn so many things you have never heard about before, and it really broadens you understanding of the development of the technology we see today and will see in the future.
I also personally liked the World Women course because I feel like your personal views might get a little challenged while you learn about certain dynamics and developments through history you haven't necesarily considered. 
I honestly think that all my courses were good, however just be aware that Social Problems was a little heavy.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: It wasn't an unexpected cost since I also experienced it last time, but but the cost of restaurant and cafées is probably higher than people assume. The reasoning is that while food in Korean more local restaurants is not too bad it quickly adds up if you are mostly having your meals outside. In addition, the café culture is really big in Korea so you often end up in a café when you are meeting up with people and cafées are usually expensive.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: Entance fees to museums are very low becaue the government wants to encourage its citizens to learn about their own history and culture. Exhibitions on the other hand and specific trendy cultural places are more expensive.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: They had one club that specifically created events for international students so you could meet other international student, there was a language lounge where you could teach other students English, there were 2 different language clubs where you would be partnered up with Korean students so you could meet and do activities and if you were learning Korean you could also practice with them.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: I suggest joining the Buddy Program and one of the language clubs. In the Buddy Program you are paired up with one Korean student and then maybe 4-6 international student, so you can both meet a Korean student and ask them about stuff and become familiar with the culture and get help with school stuff and meet other international students that are experiencing the exact same things as you are. The language clubs offer a opportunity for maybe a more personal relationship with the Korean student in the sense that it is more 1-1 so I feel there is a greater chance at gaining a Korean friend.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: In the weekends go out and see some of the cultural and historical places. Some of the museums are even free so take advantage of that, the price for entering the palaces is low as well, and they have their traditional villages which you can enter free of charge. Also keep an eye on the events happening because there is usually always something you can do or go to. And during the holidays travel! Seoul is great but it gives such a nice and more comprehensive idea of Korea and Korean culture if you travel out plus there is so many beautiful places and fun things you can experience. I would sugget to at least go to Busan, Jeonju and Jeju.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: Since it was my second time I think I had a rather easy time adjusting.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: Keep in mind many local students/Korean students live very busy lives and some might be a bit more apprehensive getting close since you might only be there for exchange (especially if it's only 1 semester). But befriend people in your classes, go to events and meet people through clubs.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: You have to get a little used to being stared a bit at. it is not as bad in Seoul and it also depends on where in Seoul you are, but people are just very fascinated and curious. Korean society is still pretty homogeneous.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: The food and the cultural mix between metropolitan and tradtional. I also find it very cool that people style-wise in clothing can almost look however they want without people flinching an eye vs. in Denmark.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
Go with an open mind and be ready to go out of your comfort zone. 
The international office or your buddy in the buddy program can help you if you need it.
Your courses can influence your experience so read up on what the courses require for you to pass, and be prepared and ready to register your courses.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: If you live off campus getting a resident card requires more documents and some of it can be a little complicated. The reason is that the university has an external firm to handle the resident cards for their students so the firm is very strict with your papers. But having said so you can always talk with the international office if you encounter any problem.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: Everything. All the experiences I have had, the people I have met, and the knowledge I have gained.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: Figuring out how to balance the workload and making sure I fully enjoyed and experienced Korea. Like I mentioned there is a consistent level of intensity in Korea due to tests, assignments and presentations throughout the semster, so you have to remind yourself that you also need to make time to go out and see thing and experience the culture.

questions.question: Any other comments?
Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
